text: There's no new infrastructure concept in this lesson. The capstone was the last piece of technical material in the course — this lesson is about doing the thing that turns "I built something" into "I understand what I built": writing it up.

Keep the first part short and concrete: what you stood up, which pieces from the course it used, and what you verified actually worked. Then write an architecture-decision-record-style reflection on scale. At ten times your capstone's size, would your storage choice and checkpoint frequency still hold up? At a hundred times, approaching solara-train's real size, would your networking assumptions and a single namespace still be enough? And what's the first thing you did by hand that would become a real liability repeated across dozens or hundreds of jobs?

Here's the whole course in six chapters. Chapter one established what any cluster has to do, regardless of the model. Chapter two covered networking — NCCL, AllReduce, InfiniBand. Chapter three covered orchestration — Kubernetes and Slurm scheduling. Chapter four covered fault tolerance — checkpointing, resuming, designing for node failure. Chapter five covered storage and data loading — sharding, storage backends, caching. And chapter six, this one, covered monitoring and cost — GPU utilization, cost attribution, alerting, and the capstone itself.

This course deliberately stayed on the infrastructure side of the line drawn back in Chapter one — what has to be true underneath a training run, not the algorithm running on top of it. Advanced LLM Training and ML Systems picks up exactly that other half: the actual techniques used to train a model like Solara-70B. If this course was about the cluster, that one is about what runs on it.
